The eight decisions, carried out¶

29 October 2026. Follows report_transitions_20261028.ipynb, section 7. For each decision: what was done, what it changed, and how it was checked. "Before" in the figures is the production of 28 October (after the first border matching); "after" is the production made for this report.

# decision what was done result
1 weight the border matching by reliability; use it to calibrate the less reliable method each fill pixel is now held to its own prediction in proportion to 1/uncertainty^2, so at a border the less reliable side moves; each feature set is first shifted by its mean mismatch at its borders with more reliable pixels (a calibration learned from the borders) in production for F770W-F1280W and F410M; on hold-out cores equal or better than equal weights, with smaller bias deep inside the cores
2 the SOFIA scale k k measured again with SOFIA's own beam profile, and tested against published totals (FORCAST, MSX) k = 1.137 kept: the restored image already matches or exceeds the published totals
3 the level drift of the feature sets explained below; a joint model of all filters without feature sets was built and tested not adopted: on hold-out cores it is no better than the feature sets with matching (worse in F770W-F1280W)
4 F410M empty centre: point source + diffuse model joint fit over the four dithers, flux checked in F405N and F480M 338-346 of the about 760 empty centre pixels per core exposure restored (where the star dominates), new METHOD 11
5 F410M ring pixels with good reads but no pipeline value refit from their reads (new METHOD 10); the spill ring takes the cross-filter model mean 27,347 pixel-exposures refit (agree with the pipeline method to 0.001 dex); the ring is filled
6 F410M low-confidence star models refit with the point source + diffuse model, kept where they validate better 697 of 1,575 replaced; their edge step falls from +0.79 to +0.01 dex
7 MIRI empty compact cores: (b) totals from other telescopes, (c) new JWST data disk fluxes estimated three ways and filled; verified; saturation of MRS and subarrays computed (b) does not verify (estimates disagree by 2-10x; with the disk, the IRS2E aperture overshoots); (c) both saturate. The disks stay empty
8 MIRI fill in the coronagraph area cause found; the mosaic now weights each exposure by its uncertainty the cause is the Lyot field, outside the ramp step's sky mask; see section 8 for the mosaic
term meaning
fill, feature set a core pixel predicted from its brightness in other filters; the feature set is the list of filters used (it shrinks where inputs saturate)
uncertainty (ERR) the expected error of a restored value in dex, from the method's own tests
border matching the correction that joins each fill region to the pixels around it without blurring it (py/match_fill.py)
hold-out core bright response-curve pixels hidden, predicted, and compared with their values
k the scale between F2100W and SOFIA's 19.7 µm image: F2100W (smoothed to 3") = k x SOFIA - b
PSF point spread function: the image of a point source made by the telescope, with its rings and six diffraction spikes
dex a factor in log10: 0.01 dex = 2.3%, 0.1 dex = 26%, 0.3 dex = a factor 2
METHOD 10, 11 new codes: 10 refit from good reads, 11 star + diffuse model

def restored(f, n, ver='after'):
    with fits.open(f'{VER[ver]}/{f}/{n}_restored.fits') as h:
        return h['SCI'].data.astype(float), h['METHOD'].data

def floor_of(n):
    with fits.open(f'{P}/miri_ramp/restored/{n}_ramp.fits') as h:
        rs, rm, rq = h['SCI'].data, h['METHOD'].data, h['Q0'].data
    inv = np.isin(rm, [2, 3]) & np.isfinite(rq) & np.isfinite(rs)
    return np.nanmedian(rs[inv & (rq >= 0.95 * np.nanmax(rq[inv]))]), rm

def show_img(ax, img, norm, title):
    cm = plt.get_cmap('magma').copy(); cm.set_bad(LIGHT)
    ax.imshow(img, origin='lower', cmap=cm, norm=norm, interpolation='nearest')
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)

def show_method(ax, m, title='method'):
    ax.imshow(m, origin='lower', cmap=ListedColormap(MC), vmin=-0.5, vmax=len(MC) - 0.5, interpolation='nearest')
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)

def method_legend(fig, codes, **kw):
    fig.legend(handles=[Patch(fc=MC[k], ec=GREY, label=METHODS[k]) for k in codes], loc='lower center', ncol=4, fontsize=10, **kw)

def window(mask, half, x0=0):
    d = ndimage.uniform_filter(mask.astype(float), 2 * half)
    d[:half], d[-half:], d[:, :x0 + half], d[:, -half:] = 0, 0, 0, 0
    cy, cx = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(d), d.shape)
    return slice(cy - half, cy + half), slice(cx - half, cx + half)

1. Border matching weighted by reliability, and calibration from the borders¶

What changed. Before, the regions of a fill were matched from the outside in: the region nearest the measured pixels took their level, the next region took the level of the first, and so on, whatever their reliability. Now all fill pixels are solved together, and each one is held to its own prediction in proportion to 1/uncertainty², where the uncertainty is the error the fill method expects for that pixel (it grows with the number of saturated inputs and with how far the pixel lies beyond the brightness range the model was trained on). Where two regions meet, the mismatch is split about as their uncertainties: a set with three times the uncertainty takes about three quarters of the step. The correction also reaches further into a less reliable region.

Calibration from the borders. Before the solve, each region is shifted as a whole by its mean mismatch at its borders with more reliable pixels (measured pixels, or sets with a smaller uncertainty). This is a calibration of that set, learned from the places where it meets better data; the solve then only joins what is left. Without it, the correction of a region fades back to the set's own (miscalibrated) level deep inside a large core.

The toy below has measured pixels on the left, a reliable set A and an unreliable set B that is 0.3 dex too high.

In [2]:
# toy: a measured border on the left (x < 8), a reliable fill region A (sigma 0.03) and an unreliable one B (sigma 0.15, set 0.3 dex too high)
yy, xx = np.mgrid[:30, :60]
truth = 4 + 0.012 * xx
fill = xx >= 8
lab = np.where(xx >= 34, 1, 0)
pred = np.where(fill, truth + np.where(lab == 1, 0.3, 0.02), truth)
sig = np.where(lab == 1, 0.15, 0.03)
V = {'equal weights': match(pred, ~fill, fill, lab, 30.)[0],
     'weighted by uncertainty': match(pred, ~fill, fill, lab, 30., sig=sig)[0],
     'weighted + calibrated': match(pred, ~fill, fill, lab, 30., sig=sig, calibrate=True)[0]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.6))
ax.plot(xx[15], truth[15], color=GREY, lw=4, label='truth')
ax.plot(xx[15], pred[15], color=INK, lw=1.2, label='fill before matching')
for (k, v), c in zip(V.items(), (YELLOW, BLUE, RED)):
    ax.plot(xx[15], v[15], color=c, lw=1.6, label=k)
ax.axvspan(-1, 8, color=LIGHT, alpha=0.9, lw=0); ax.axvspan(34, 60, color='#f3e3d8', alpha=0.6, lw=0)
ax.text(1, 5.05, 'measured', color=MUTED, fontsize=9); ax.text(12, 5.05, 'set A (reliable)', color=MUTED, fontsize=9); ax.text(36, 5.05, 'set B (unreliable, 0.3 dex high)', color=MUTED, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(-1, 60); ax.set_ylim(3.95, 5.12)
ax.set_xlabel('pixel'); ax.set_ylabel('log10 brightness'); ax.set_title('border matching with and without the uncertainty of each set'); ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='lower right')
plt.tight_layout()

Reading the figure. With equal weights, the 0.3 dex mismatch of set B is shared with set A, which is pulled up near the border. Weighted by uncertainty, set A stays where it is and set B comes down; deep inside B the correction fades. With the calibration, all of set B is shifted first, so it sits at the right level everywhere.

On real data (hold-out cores, 16 exposures per filter; bias and spread of log10(fill / hidden curve value), dex):

2. The SOFIA scale k¶

What k is. SOFIA's FORCAST camera imaged W51 at 19.7 µm with a 3" beam, without saturating. Our F2100W image (21 µm) and SOFIA's do not measure the same thing: the bands differ, the calibrations differ, and SOFIA's image is about 4.5 times blurrier (a 3" beam against 0.67"). To compare them, the F2100W image is first smoothed to SOFIA's resolution; then, over sky that F2100W measured directly (no restored pixels), the two are related by a straight line: F2100W (smoothed) = k × SOFIA − b, fitted as k = 1.137 ± 0.053 and b = 1079 MJy/sr. In words: for the same sky, F2100W is about 14% brighter than SOFIA, minus a small offset. The pin then rescales the F2100W fill so that every 3" patch of a core equals k × SOFIA − b there. k therefore sets the level of every restored F2100W core.

What was tested (study: production/anchors/, README there):

  1. SOFIA's beam. The pin smooths F2100W with a 3" Gaussian. SOFIA's real beam has more light in wide wings: at 4.5" from IRS2 the SOFIA profile is at 25% of its peak, a 3" Gaussian at 0.2%. No isolated point source exists in the map to measure the beam cleanly, so the wing fraction is uncertain (IRS2 itself is extended).
  2. k refitted with beams that have 8%, 15% and 30% of their light in wings: 1.147, 1.118 and 1.011 (the Gaussian refit gives 1.159). The bright response-curve pixels prefer 1.21-1.25. The left panel shows these values with their jackknife errors, the right panel the F2100W/SOFIA ratio each implies as a function of brightness.
  3. Totals from other telescopes (right figure). In FORCAST's published 3.84" aperture on IRS2E, the restored F2100W holds 918 Jy (with the empty disk left out) against 817 Jy published and 838 Jy in the SOFIA map. In an 18.3" beam on IRS2, the restored image holds 1973 Jy against 1658 Jy from MSX at 21.3 µm (1568 Jy after converting MSX's band to F2100W's); the SOFIA map itself gives 2103 Jy there.

display(Image(filename=f'{P}/anchors/figs/A2_k.png', width=1000))
display(Image(filename=f'{P}/anchors/figs/A3_closure.png', width=1000))

Decision: k = 1.137 is kept. The restored image already sits at or above every published total (1.12x FORCAST in the IRS2E aperture, 1.19x MSX in 18"), so a larger k (1.2-1.25, as the bright curve pixels prefer) would add light that the totals do not support. The 0.04-0.08 dex deficit that the hold-out cores showed inside the brightest cores is more likely due to the beam wings and to the empty disks (the pin leaves them out of its 3" sums, while SOFIA sees their light) than to k. The systematic uncertainty of k is about ±0.1 (±0.04 dex in the level).

SOFIA and MSX differ by 27% in the 18" beam. That spread between the two calibrations bounds how well any external total can set the F2100W level.

3. The level drift of the feature sets¶

What it means. A cross-filter fill predicts a core pixel from its brightness in the other filters with a straight line in log brightness: log F2100W = c + Σ b_i log F_i. The line is fitted on pixels that are fainter than the cores. On the response-curve pixels the fill never saw, its error can be measured as a function of brightness: if the line were right everywhere, the error would stay at 0. It does not: it drifts with brightness, and differently for each feature set. That is the "level drift". The figure shows it per feature set, for the fills as they were before the matching.

What causes it.

  • A straight line extrapolated past its data. The cores are 2-100 times brighter than any pixel in the fit. Real colours likely bend at high brightness: warmer dust in the cores raises 21 µm relative to the shorter filters, the 10 µm silicate absorption can deepen, and the PAH bands (7.7, 11.3, 12.7 µm) and the [Ne II] line can weaken relative to the dust continuum. A straight line misses such a bend, so its error grows with brightness.
  • Each feature set bends its own way. Each set is a separate line using different filters. Where a filter is dropped because it saturated, the next set implicitly assumes a typical value for it, which near a core is too low. At a border between two sets the two lines disagree by however much their drifts differ there: those are the steps of the first report.
In [5]:

Reading the figure. The set with the most filters stays within about ±0.1 dex at all brightnesses. The smaller sets are off by 0.1-0.3 dex already below half the floor, and the gap grows with brightness. In F2100W most sets predict too much (the curve value is below the model); the sets without F770W and F1280W (F560W+F1000W+NIRCam, F560W+F1000W) drift fastest, to 0.4-0.5 dex at 1.3-1.4 times the floor. In F1280W most sets predict too little, the opposite sign. The spread between the sets at the floor, 0.25-0.4 dex, is the size of the steps that were seen at set borders.

What was done: one joint model without feature sets (production/miri_xband/joint.py). All filters, target included, are modelled together as one multivariate normal distribution in log brightness, fitted on all 16 exposures of the target at once. Each value enters in one of three ways: as measured; as a lower limit where that filter is saturated (its brightness at the edge of its saturated region, extended inward); or as unknown where a filter does not cover the pixel. The core pixels themselves are lower limits too. The fit is an EM algorithm: the measured values condition the normal exactly, and each lower limit is applied by matching the moments of the truncated normal. Because no filter is ever dropped, there are no sets and no set borders: where an input filter saturates, it changes from "measured at its saturation level" to "at least its saturation level", and the prediction changes continuously. Each pixel also gets its own uncertainty, larger where more inputs are only lower limits. A self-check on simulated data recovers the true mean and covariance and gives unbiased predictions for censored rows.

Test on hold-out cores (curve pixels above min(median curve value, 0.55 × floor) hidden from both fits; bias and spread in dex):

Reading the table. The joint model is no better than the feature sets with border matching: about equal in F2100W (after SOFIA: -0.040 / 0.071 against -0.042 / 0.065 dex), worse in F770W (spread 0.050 against 0.033), F1000W (0.146 against 0.086) and F1280W (0.047 against 0.038). Two reasons: one joint normal cannot follow colours that bend with brightness any better than the straight lines can (F1000W, whose production fill has colour-dependent terms, loses most); and the lower limits of saturated inputs carry little information deep inside a core. The joint model removes the set borders by construction, but the border matching already removes them in the image, with better accuracy.

Decision: the production fill keeps the feature sets, joined by the weighted, calibrated border matching of section 1. The joint model and its hold-out fills stay in production/miri_xband/joint*/ for reference. What would reduce the drift itself is a model whose colours can bend with brightness, trained on the response-curve pixels near the top (as done for F2100W): the F1000W "quadc" model is a first version of that.

4-5. F410M: the point source in the centre, and the ring¶

Point source + diffuse model (study and products: production/psf_f410m/, README there). The empty centre of the brightest F410M core holds one bright point source: its six diffraction spikes run across the measured pixels around the core. The model is that source (the F410M PSF from STPSF for the observation date in the headers, 2025-05-06, with free flux and position) plus the diffuse emission around it, taken from the restored image beyond 12 px. It was fitted jointly to the four dithers that see the core (one flux, one position per exposure), with the empty pixels entering as lower limits (each is above its first-read ceiling).

  • Flux. The same fit on the wings and spikes in F405N and F480M (also saturated in the centre), interpolated to 4.1 µm, gives 1.48 × 10^8 MJy/sr px; F410M itself gives 1.29-1.46 × 10^8 depending on how the fill near the star is treated. Adopted: 1.40 × 10^8 MJy/sr px (about 13 Jy) ± 7%.
  • Which pixels. A pixel is restored only where the point source carries at least 75% of the model and the model lies above the pixel's ceiling: 338-346 of the about 760 empty pixels per core exposure, out to 24 px from the star (median uncertainty 0.074 dex). Farther out the core is nebula, not star, and those pixels stay empty.

The ring had two parts:

  • Pixels with good reads but no pipeline value (the pipeline flagged them "do not use"; most are isolated bad pixels, not part of a ring): their rate is now refit from their own unsaturated reads exactly as the pipeline would (study: production/nircam_refit/). On pixels that do have a pipeline value, the refit agrees with it to 0.001 dex. 27,347 of 44,985 such pixel-exposures get a value; the rest sit on the detector border, lack a linearity correction, or are contaminated by charge from saturated neighbours. METHOD 10.
  • The spill ring (pixels next to a ceiling pixel, whose first read holds charge spilled from it; their sky is below the ceiling): they now take the cross-filter model mean, or the point-source model where the star dominates, and the border matching joins them to both sides.

The figure shows the core exposure before (production of 28 October) and after, on the same colour scale, with the method of every pixel.

Reading the figure. The centre now holds the star: a peak of 1.5 × 10^7 MJy/sr, with the PSF's rings. The ring of empty pixels between the fill and the measured pixels is gone, replaced by the model mean (orange). The scattered empty pixels across the field (dark red dots before) are now refit from their good reads (green dots). What remains empty (dark red) lies next to the star, where the star carries less than 75% of the model, and in three small patches of the nebula where every input of the cross-filter fill is saturated.

The next figure gives the restored values against the distance from the star: the point-source model (red) falls steeply to the level of the existing fill at 12-15 px, where the two join. The spill-ring pixels the model takes (blue) lie below the fill at the same distance, as they should: their sky is below the first-read ceiling, and the fill's is above it.

6. F410M low-confidence star models refit¶

The low-confidence star models sat 0.44-0.52 dex above the measured pixels around them. Every one of the 1,575 in F410M was refit with the point source + diffuse model, using the unsaturated pixels around it and, where the first read was saturated, the ceiling as a lower limit. A refit replaces the old model only where it validates better: it must lower the step at its edge by at least 0.05 dex, not worsen the agreement with the same star in other dithers by more than 0.03 dex, and pass the fit-quality cuts. 697 of 1,575 passed (46 on the A-detector, 651 on B). For those, the edge step goes from +0.79 to +0.007 dex and the aperture error against other dithers from 0.047 to 0.017 dex. The others keep the old model (their edge step is smaller, +0.34 dex median).

Left: the edge step of every star, old model and refit; right: the star's aperture sum against the other dithers. Below: six of the replaced stars, before and after, with a row of pixels through each.

In [10]:

display(Image(filename=f'{P}/psf_f410m/figures/fig3_refit_stars.png', width=1100))

Reading the figures. Many of the replaced "stars" are single pixels flagged as saturated where nothing bright exists (a hot pixel or a cosmic ray): the old model put a spike, or a hole, there; the refit finds no star and continues the sky. For real stars the refit removes the edge step and agrees better with the other dithers. METHOD 11 covers all three uses of the model (centre, spill ring, refit stars).

7. The empty MIRI compact cores: results of (b) and (c)¶

The empty disks are the brightest compact cores, where every input filter of the cross-filter fill saturates: 6 in F2100W, 7 in F1280W, 2 in F1000W, 5 in F770W (none in F560W). The largest is IRS2E (19:23:40.12 +14:31:05.8, 366 px in F2100W). Study: production/anchors/.

(b) Totals from other telescopes. Each disk's flux was estimated three ways, wherever possible:

  • flat floor: the brightness of the ring around the disk times the disk's area (a lower-limit-like value);
  • SOFIA residual: k × SOFIA − b in beams centred on the disk, minus the restored flux around it;
  • T-ReCS + floor: the published compact flux at 24.6 µm (Gemini T-ReCS, 0.5"), scaled to 21 µm, plus the floor for the diffuse part. MSX could not be used per disk: its 18" beam is dominated by the restored surroundings, and the residual came out negative. For IRS2E in F2100W: floor 215 Jy, SOFIA residual 139-172 Jy, T-ReCS + floor 274 Jy; adopted 243 Jy ± 0.15 dex. The figure shows all disks.

Verification. The disks were filled with the ring's radial profile continued inward and scaled to the adopted flux (continuous with the ring by construction). Then the F2100W disks were pinned to SOFIA together with the ring, so that SOFIA's total is shared between them. The table checks IRS2E in the four exposures that see it:

Reading. The disk peak is about 2.7 × 10^6 MJy/sr (0.8 Jy in one 0.11" pixel), the brightest restored pixel nearby 6.2 × 10^6 MJy/sr. Even the smallest subarray (SUB64, 0.085 s frames) would collect 40-80 times its per-pixel limit, SUB128 60-130, SUB256 160-330; the saturated area would still be 6-8" across. MRS channel 4 would receive about 15 times its limit within 1.5" of IRS2E. (c): both options saturate on the brightest cores.

Decision: the disks stay empty (METHOD 8) in production. The disk fills and the jointly pinned F2100W are kept as files (production/miri_disks/, production/miri_xband/filled_kd/) for anyone who wants an estimate with a large error.

8. The fill in the coronagraph area: cause, and the weighted mosaic¶

Cause. The low fill pixels of the last report are not in the four-quadrant coronagraph panes. They sit in the Lyot coronagraph field, the top-left corner of the MIRI detector (rows 751-1016, columns 11-276). That field has a flat field and the pipeline calibrates it like the main field, so its unsaturated pixels agree with the main field of other exposures. But the ramp-inversion step (the response curve) runs only on the main imager field and the four-quadrant panes. In the Lyot field a saturated pixel therefore gets no response-curve value and is never recognised as a ceiling pixel, so it gets no floor either: it keeps the raw cross-filter fill. The F1280W fill runs low at the bright end (section 3), and with no curve pixels around and no floor, nothing corrects it there. In fainter sky the same pixels agree with the other exposures.

The figure marks where the ramp step runs, and the fill pixels in the Lyot field that have neither a curve value nor a floor (red).

Fix: the mosaic weights each exposure by its uncertainty. Every restored pixel carries its uncertainty (ERR, dex); unsaturated and pipeline values count as 0.01 dex. The mosaic is now the weighted mean with weight 1/ERR², so where another dither measured the same sky (or restored it with the response curve), that value outweighs a fill, typically by 10 to 100 times. The table compares the mosaic with the response-curve value of the same sky in other exposures, at the sky pixels where one exposure has a Lyot-field fill:

Reading the table. With equal weights the mosaic sat 0.010 to 0.021 dex below the response-curve values of the same sky at these pixels; weighted by uncertainty it sits 0.003 to 0.005 dex below, with about the same spread. The fill of a single exposure is unchanged by the mosaic: in F770W exposure 002002_0210d_00001 (3,347 Lyot-field fill pixels) it lies 0.107 dex below the curve values of the other exposures. It was 0.086 dex below on 28 October; the calibration of section 1 moved it down by about 0.02 dex, because in the Lyot field its only borders are with unsaturated pipeline pixels, where the fill agrees, while its deficit grows towards the centre of the core, where no border sees it. The main-field fill of every F770W exposure is unchanged (0.01 to 0.04 dex above the curve values; fill_rc_by_exp.py). So the single exposures still carry the Lyot deficit, and the mosaic no longer does.

The root fix is to run the ramp step in the Lyot field too; it needs the detector offsets of the ramp model there and a rerun of the ramp restoration (an item for the next step).

9. Final products and checks¶

Mosaics (all exposures combined, weighted by uncertainty) before (production of 28 October) and after, on the same colour scale.

def mos(ver, f):
    with fits.open(f'{VER[ver]}/mosaic_{f}.fits') as h:
        return h['AFTER'].data.astype(float), h['METHOD'].data
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(14, 21))
for r, f in zip(ax, ['F2100W', 'F1280W', 'F410M']):

    sl = window(np.isin(ma, [6, 9, 11]), 110 if f != 'F410M' else 160)
    v = np.nanpercentile(a[sl], [3, 99.8]); norm = LogNorm(*v)
    show_img(r[0], b[sl], norm, f'{f} mosaic before'); show_img(r[1], a[sl], norm, f'{f} mosaic after')
plt.tight_layout()

Reading the mosaics.

  • F2100W. The level and the structure match the production of 28 October. The new mosaic has a few dark dots in the core, explained below.
  • F1280W. The core next to the empty disk is brighter. The calibration of section 1 moved the fill up towards the response-curve values of the same sky, and the empty disk stays empty (section 7).
  • F410M. The empty centre of the brightest core is mostly filled by the star + diffuse model (section 4), and the dotted outline of the spill ring is gone. Grey patches remain where the star does not dominate (section 10). The isolated white dots in the field are pixels that are empty in every exposure, the same before and after.

Two fixes to the mosaic, found while checking it. Weighting by uncertainty lets a value with a small uncertainty set the mosaic. Isolated dark pixels in the weighted F2100W mosaic led to two values that should not have that weight:

  1. NON_SCIENCE pixels. MIRI keeps a raw number in a 14 × 50 pixel block of every exposure (rows 294-307, columns 301-350; 695 pixels), flagged NON_SCIENCE: it is not sky. With no restoration uncertainty it outweighed the fill of the same sky in the other exposures. The merge now leaves these pixels without a value.
  2. Restored outliers. Response-curve values near the MIRI detector edges run low: up to 1.7 dex below the same sky in the other exposures, which sit at the ceiling there. With an uncertainty of a few hundredths of a dex, one such value set the mosaic. The mosaic now leaves out a restored value that lies more than 0.3 dex (a factor 2) from the mean of at least two other exposures at its sky pixel and is the most deviant value there. Measured values are never left out, and only values with an uncertainty below 0.3 dex take part. A first version without this last condition let three low-confidence star models (0.6 dex uncertainty, 1.4 dex below the curve and fill) outvote a single good curve value; the condition fixes that. Values left out: F2100W 338, F1280W 119, F770W 4, F1000W 0, F560W 28 and F410M 1,025 sky pixels.

Dark pixels left. Pixels more than 0.1 dex below both their 5 × 5 neighbourhood and the equal-weight mosaic of 28 October: F2100W 14 (39 with the first fix alone), F410M 14, F560W 3, F1280W 1, F770W and F1000W none. Each F2100W pixel holds a curve value near a detector edge that sits 0.2-0.3 dex below six fills of the same sky, inside the 0.3 dex limit, and it lies 0.10-0.17 dex below its neighbours in the mosaic. Thirteen of them are the dark dots in the F2100W panel above. A lower limit would remove them, but it would also leave out F410M star models whose uncertainty is about 0.12 dex. The cause is the response of the ramp model near the edges, which section 10 lists as remaining work. Across the curve and fill area the new mosaic has fewer such dips than the mosaic of 28 October (32 against 53). In F410M and F560W a measured value next to a star peak outweighs restored values of the same sky. Dithers sample a star peak at different places, so these values differ without either being wrong, and the measured value is the better one.

Checks against the other exposures (dithers: a restored pixel against the same sky in other exposures; same sky: the mean over exposures of one method against another; median ± half-width in dex, number):

In [16]:
def chk(ver, f):
    d = pd.read_csv(f'{VER[ver]}/check_{f}.csv'); c = pd.read_csv(f'{VER[ver]}/kinds/consistency_{f}.csv')
    out = {}
    for comp, meth in (('pixel, vs response curve', 'cross-filter fill'), ('pixel, vs restored', 'cross-filter fill'), ('pixel, vs restored', 'cross-filter fill, low confidence'),
                       ('pixel, vs restored', 'star + diffuse model'), ('pixel, vs measured', 'refit from good reads'), ('pixel, vs restored', 'refit from good reads'),
                       ('star aperture, vs measured', 'star model, low confidence'), ('star aperture, vs measured', 'star + diffuse model')):
        s = d[(d.comparison == comp) & (d.method == meth)]
        if len(s) and s.n.iloc[0] >= 30:
            out[f'dithers: {meth} {comp.replace("pixel, ", "")}'] = f'{s.median_dex.iloc[0]:+.3f} ± {s.halfwidth_dex.iloc[0]:.3f} ({int(s.n.iloc[0]):,})'
    for i, j in (('response curve', 'cross-filter fill'), ('cross-filter fill', 'cross-filter fill, low confidence')):
        s = c[(c.method_i == i) & (c.method_j == j)]
        if len(s) and s.n.iloc[0] >= 50:
            out[f'same sky: {i} vs {j}'] = f'{s.median_dex.iloc[0]:+.3f} ± {s.halfwidth_dex.iloc[0]:.3f} ({int(s.n.iloc[0]):,})'
    return out
rows = [dict(filter=f, check=k, ver=ver, text=t) for f in ['F770W', 'F1000W', 'F1280W', 'F2100W', 'F410M'] for ver in ('before', 'after') for k, t in chk(ver, f).items()]
pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot(index=['filter', 'check'], columns='ver', values='text')[['before', 'after']].fillna('')

Reading the table.

  • F1280W. The fill moved closer to the response-curve values of the same sky. Against curve pixels in other exposures its spread fell from 0.123 to 0.082 dex; the same-sky offset fell from +0.143 to +0.122 dex; fill against fill in other exposures from 0.039 to 0.028 dex.
  • F1000W, F2100W. Unchanged within 0.005 dex. F2100W keeps the SOFIA level; the F1000W fill-to-fill spread fell from 0.037 to 0.032 dex.
  • F770W. The offset against the curve values grew, from -0.067 to -0.089 dex (same sky: +0.083 to +0.105). Section 8 traces it to one exposure, whose Lyot-field fill the calibration moved down by about 0.02 dex; the main-field fill of every F770W exposure is unchanged.
  • F410M, refit from good reads (section 5). These pixels agree with the measured values of the same sky to +0.000 ± 0.017 dex (27,330 pixels), as close as two measured values of the brightest 1% of the sky (+0.001 ± 0.015).
  • F410M, cross-filter fill. 5,456 fill pixels now have a measured value of the same sky in another exposure, and they agree with it to +0.001 ± 0.014 dex. On 28 October there were 52, at +0.52 dex: most were spill-ring pixels, which now take the cross-filter model mean. Fill against fill in other exposures spreads more than before (accepted sets 0.016 to 0.022 dex; low-confidence sets 0.017 to 0.039 dex) over a sample that doubled with the spill ring. The accepted and low-confidence fill of the same sky now differ by 0.022 dex (was 0.014) with a spread of 0.060 (was 0.028). This fits the calibration of section 1, which moved the two sets in opposite directions (+0.01 to +0.06 dex and -0.03 to 0.00). Where both cover a sky pixel, the mosaic leans on the accepted set through its smaller uncertainty (median 0.04 dex against 0.14, a weight about 12 times larger).
  • F410M, star + diffuse model (section 4). Star apertures agree with the exposures that measured the star to +0.003 ± 0.007 dex (760 stars). Pixel by pixel the spread against other restorations is 0.167 dex, because the peak of a star changes with where it falls on a pixel; the aperture sum removes that.
  • F410M, remaining low-confidence star models (section 6). Their apertures sit +0.011 ± 0.018 dex from the measured exposures (577 stars); on 28 October the full set sat at +0.029 ± 0.028 (1,270).

Steps at the borders (excess step with the local slope removed, pixel-pair weighted mean of |median| per exposure, dex; "before" is the production of 28 October, already border-matched):

In [17]:
def class_of(a, b):
    s = {a, b}
    if a == b: return None
    if all(t.startswith('fill set') for t in s): return 'fill set -> fill set'
    if any(t.startswith('response curve') for t in s) and any(t.startswith('fill set') for t in s): return 'curve -> fill'
    if 'unsaturated or pipeline value' in s and 'star model, low confidence' in s: return 'pipeline -> star model, low confidence'
    if 'unsaturated or pipeline value' in s and 'star + diffuse model' in s: return 'pipeline -> star + diffuse model'
    if any(t.startswith('fill set') for t in s) and 'star + diffuse model' in s: return 'fill -> star + diffuse model'
    if 'unsaturated or pipeline value' in s and any(t.startswith('fill set') for t in s): return 'pipeline -> fill'
    return None
rows = []
for ver, d in (('before', f'{P}/final/transitions/steps_after'), ('after', f'{DEC}/steps_after')):
    for f in ['F2100W', 'F1280W', 'F1000W', 'F770W', 'F410M']:
        s = pd.read_csv(f'{d}_{f}.csv'); s['cls'] = [class_of(a, b) for a, b in zip(s.a, s.b)]; s = s.dropna(subset=['cls'])
        g = s.assign(w=s.n * s.median_dex.abs()).groupby('cls').agg(n=('n', 'sum'), w=('w', 'sum'))
        for c, r in g.iterrows():
            if r.n >= 200: rows.append(dict(filter=f, border=c, ver=ver, jump=r.w / r.n))
pd.DataFrame(rows).pivot_table(index=['filter', 'border'], columns='ver', values='jump')[['before', 'after']].round(3)

10. What remains¶

item why what it would take
ramp step in the Lyot field its saturated pixels get no response-curve value and no floor; single exposures carry a fill 0.1 dex low there (section 8) the detector offsets of the ramp model in that field, and a rerun of the ramp restoration and of the merge
MIRI response curve near the detector edges curve values there run low, up to 1.7 dex below the same sky in other exposures; the mosaic leaves out those beyond 0.3 dex, and about ten F2100W sky pixels keep a dip of 0.2-0.3 dex from smaller deficits (section 9) the ramp model's response near the edges, from pixels that saturate there and not in another dither
a calibration that depends on depth the border calibration fixes the level where a core meets better pixels; a deficit that grows towards the centre stays (F1000W: 0.2 dex low 10-20 px inside the hold-out cores; the F770W Lyot fill) learn the bias against distance from the border or against brightness on the hold-out cores, and test it the same way
F410M empty centre where the star does not dominate about 2,200 pixels per core exposure stay not restored, among them about 420 of the 760 empty centre pixels a diffuse model good enough to stand on its own there (it is checked only where the star dominates)
F410M low-confidence star models 878 of 1,575 stay; their border with pipeline pixels still steps by 0.38 dex refit them with a model that allows a nearby second source, or flag them
